functions; a part class from `fr.parts` rejects it when the type checker runs.

```python
from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr


class Feed(NamedTuple):
    X1: fr.TerminalStrip


@fr.unit("demo-supply-strip", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="first", by="AB")
def supply_strip(d):
    x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 2, interface=True)
    return Feed(x1)
```

```python
import subprocess
import sys
from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr

subprocess.run(
    [sys.executable, "-m", "fransys", "parts-module", "demo_parts", "demo_typed.py"], check=True
)
sys.path.insert(0, ".")
import demo_typed as P


class Io(NamedTuple):
    X1: P.DEMO_CONN_2P


@fr.unit("demo-supply-box", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="first", by="AB")
def box(d: fr.Design) -> Io:
    x1 = d.device("X1", P.DEMO_CONN_2P, interface=True)
    return Io(x1)
```

Annotate each device field with the generated part class it was built from, as `P.DEMO_CONN_2P`
above. A bare `fr.Device` hides the part's functions from the type checker.

```python
from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr


class Io(NamedTuple):
    X7: fr.Device


@fr.unit("demo-board", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="first", by="AB")
def board(d):
    return Io(d.device("X7", "DEMO-CONN-2P", interface=True))


@fr.unit("demo-assembly", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="first", by="AB")
def assembly(d):
    return Io(d.add(board, "U2").X7)  # the board's connector is the assembly's interface too


d = fr.design("demo_parts")
unit = d.add(assembly, "U1")
d.cable("W1", "DEMO-CBL-4G1.5").core(1, d.device("P1", "DEMO-CONN-2P")[1], unit.X7[1])
assert not [f for f in fr.build(d).findings if f.code == "UNIT_BOUNDARY_BYPASSED"]
```

A unit's own `unused=` is the unit's fact. A carrier that leaves some boundary points of a unit it adds open for another carrier
declares them itself. `d.unused(pc.x3[3], pc.x4_1)` takes typed points of the returned fields, never a string.
The same call takes a port, `d.unused(m1.minus)`: the port is open on purpose and `FUNCTION_HALF_CONNECTED` stays silent for it.
A point or port that is wired gives `UNUSED_POINT_WIRED`, one that is no boundary point gives `UNUSED_NOT_BOUNDARY`,
and a point listed twice raises `UNUSED_LISTED_TWICE`.

```python
from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr


class CabinetIo(NamedTuple):
    x3: fr.TerminalStrip


@fr.unit("demo-cabinet", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="first", by="AB")
def cabinet(d: fr.Design) -> CabinetIo:
    return CabinetIo(d.terminal_strip("X3", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 4, interface=(1, 2, 3, 4)))


d = fr.design("demo_parts")
pc = d.add(cabinet, "PC")
lamp = d.device("H1", "DEMO-LAMP-24")
d.series(pc.x3[1], lamp["1"], wire=("RD", 2.5))
d.series(pc.x3[2], lamp["2"], wire=("BU", 2.5))
m1, m2 = d.device("U1", "DEMO-MODULE-2P-COM4"), d.device("U2", "DEMO-MODULE-2P-COM4")
d.series(m1.plus, m2.plus, wire=("RD", 1.5))
d.unused(pc.x3[3], pc.x3[4], m1.minus, m2.minus)  # two boundary points and two ports left open on purpose
assert not [f for f in fr.check(fr.build(d)) if f.code in {"BOUNDARY_UNCONNECTED", "FUNCTION_HALF_CONNECTED"}]
```

## Variants and revised copies

A variant is a parameter of your own builders, never a Fransys feature. Fransys has no variant hook,
and nothing patches `fr.Design`. A revised copy of a unit is a factory around `@fr.unit`: a function that
takes the name, the revision and the variant, and returns the decorated unit.

`@fr.unit` returns a `fr.UnitDef[R]`, where `R` is the tuple or NamedTuple your build returns. Annotate a parameter or a return with it.

```python
from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr


class BoardIo(NamedTuple):
    X1: fr.Device


def board_unit(name: str, revision: int, *, pins: str = "DEMO-CONN-2P") -> fr.UnitDef[BoardIo]:
    @fr.unit(name, revision=revision, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="issue", by="AB")
    def board(d: fr.Design) -> BoardIo:
        return BoardIo(d.device("X1", pins, interface=True))

    return board


first = board_unit("demo-io-board", 1)
revised = board_unit("demo-io-board-r2", 2, pins="DEMO-CONN-4P")
d = fr.design("demo_parts")
u1 = d.add(first, "U1")
u2 = d.add(revised, "U2")
d.cable("W1", "DEMO-CBL-4G1.5").core(1, d.device("P1", "DEMO-CONN-2P")[1], u1.X1[1])
d.cable("W2", "DEMO-CBL-4G1.5").core(1, d.device("P2", "DEMO-CONN-2P")[1], u2.X1[1])
assert len(fr.derive.units(fr.build(d).model)) == 2
```

## Reaching a unit from outside

A container reaches a unit's connector with a cable core onto its pin, `d.cable("W1", P.CBL).core(1, plug[1], io.X1[1])`.
Mates are refused in 0.22 (`MATES_DISABLED`). A `d.series` wire onto a male or female connector of a nested
unit gives the warning `CONNECTOR_WIRED_WITHOUT_MATE`; a cable core onto it and a screw terminal give none.

A unit built alone, with nothing outside it, leaves its interface unconnected, and
`BOUNDARY_UNCONNECTED` stays silent: an open interface is what the next integrator connects.
The finding fires once the unit sits inside something larger and an interface device is neither
wired nor `unused`.

Nets do not cross a unit boundary. Join across it with `d.series(a, b, wire=...)`. A net with pins in two units that no wire joins gives
`NET_ACROSS_UNIT_BOUNDARY_OPEN` or `NET_ACROSS_UNIT_BOUNDARY_JOINED`, which names the net and the boundary pin.

The container below wires terminal 1 of strip unit `U1` to terminal 1 of strip unit `U2`. The wire
goes through the container, and each unit's strip is seen from outside through its interface field `x1`.

```python
from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr


class StripIo(NamedTuple):
    x1: fr.TerminalStrip


@fr.unit("demo-supply-strip", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="first", by="AB")
def supply(d):
    return StripIo(d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 2, interface=(1,)))


@fr.unit("demo-load-strip", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="first", by="AB")
def load(d):
    return StripIo(d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 2, interface=(1,)))


class Cabinet(NamedTuple):
    pass


@fr.unit("demo-cabinet", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="first", by="AB")
def cabinet(d):
    a = d.add(supply, "U1")
    b = d.add(load, "U2")
    d.series(a.x1[1], b.x1[1], wire=("BU", 0.75))
    return Cabinet()


d = fr.design("demo_parts")
d.add(cabinet, "U1")
assert not [f for f in fr.check(fr.build(d)) if f.severity is fr.Severity.ERROR]
```

A nested unit with a harness line at one of its interfaces draws on its parent's page as one
outline, with its columns above and below it. A unit with none keeps its usual frame. Inside stand
only its interfaces, title and revision. Each line-end interface is a connector box on the outline,
and the harness plug touches it from outside. The columns feeding top-edge interfaces stand above,
and those leaving bottom-edge interfaces stand below. Layout picks each interface's edge. A
single-wire interface keeps its column's flow. Harness interfaces split evenly, with supply-heavy
ones on top. The group stands at the left of its page and stays whole on one page.

## Tags and places

Instance tags count up inside their parent, the cabinet unit: `-U1`, `-U2`, with no prefix. One level
up, in the top design, they print behind the cabinet's own tag: `-U1-U2-X1`. A circuit, such as one
pump's or one string's, is a function block (`with d.function(...)`), never a place. A place is where
units and field devices stand: a room, a site, a ship's hold.

## A board with parts mounted on it

A part installed on the board as part of its assembly (pressed or bolted onto its copper) is a
child of the board: `parent=board`. The enclosure receptacles are not part of the board, so they
stay in the enclosure. For the board's parts and nets to draw, the board must be the only top-level
device of its own unit. So make the board assembly its own unit: the board plus its mounted parts.
Nest that unit in the enclosure unit, which holds the receptacles. Join the board's interface
connector to the receptacles with `d.series(..., wire=...)`; the wire crosses the unit
boundary and draws as a boundary connection. The board's parts draw on the board unit's pages, not
the enclosure's. A board that shares its unit with another top-level device draws as a black box,
and `BOARD_NETS_NOT_DRAWN` is an ERROR that names its dropped nets.

## Task: a board unit in a cabinet

The cabinet is the unit that holds the boards. It holds two identical io boards, `U1` and `U2`. A
board has one connector the cabinet plugs into and one spare connector left open. Both boards share
one release; each instance prints its own tag, so no designation repeats. The same tag twice in one
unit gives `PRODUCT_DESIGNATION_DUPLICATE`. The cabinet is added to the top design.

```python
# easy: board units in a cabinet
from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr


class Io(NamedTuple):
    X1: fr.Device


@fr.unit("demo-io-board", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="first release", by="AB")
def board(d):
    x1 = d.device("X1", "DEMO-CONN-2P", interface=True)
    d.device("X2", "DEMO-CONN-2P", interface=True, unused=True)
    return Io(x1)


class Cabinet(NamedTuple):
    pass


@fr.unit(
    "demo-cabinet",
    revision=1,
    interface_version=1,
    date="2026-01-01",
    text="first release",
    by="AB",
    title="Demo cabinet",
    number="DC-1",
)
def cabinet(c):
    io1 = c.add(board, "U1")
    io2 = c.add(board, "U2")
    p1 = c.device("P1", "DEMO-CONN-2P")
    p2 = c.device("P2", "DEMO-CONN-2P")
    c.cable("W1", "DEMO-CBL-4G1.5").core(1, p1[1], io1.X1[1])
    c.cable("W2", "DEMO-CBL-4G1.5").core(1, p2[1], io2.X1[1])
    return Cabinet()


d = fr.design("demo_parts")
d.add(cabinet, "U1")
```

The efficient level builds the same model. The cabinet's boards and plugs come from one loop.

```python
# efficient: board units in a cabinet
from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr


class Io(NamedTuple):
    X1: fr.Device


@fr.unit("demo-io-board", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="first release", by="AB")
def board(d):
    x1 = d.device("X1", "DEMO-CONN-2P", interface=True)
    d.device("X2", "DEMO-CONN-2P", interface=True, unused=True)
    return Io(x1)


class Cabinet(NamedTuple):
    pass


@fr.unit(
    "demo-cabinet",
    revision=1,
    interface_version=1,
    date="2026-01-01",
    text="first release",
    by="AB",
    title="Demo cabinet",
    number="DC-1",
)
def cabinet(c):
    for n in (1, 2):
        io = c.add(board, f"U{n}")
        c.cable(f"W{n}", "DEMO-CBL-4G1.5").core(1, c.device(f"P{n}", "DEMO-CONN-2P")[1], io.X1[1])
    return Cabinet()


d = fr.design("demo_parts")
d.add(cabinet, "U1")
```

A loop of boards takes a tag for each instance, and a `name=` is the identity its number holds to in later releases.

```python
@fr.unit(
    "demo-io-board",
    revision=1,
    interface_version=1,
    date="2026-01-01",
    text="first release",
    by="AB",
)
def numbered_board(d):
    return Io(d.device("X1", "DEMO-CONN-2P", interface=True))


@fr.unit(
    "demo-numbered-cabinet",
    revision=1,
    interface_version=1,
    date="2026-01-01",
    text="first release",
    by="AB",
    title="Numbered cabinet",
    number="NC-1",
)
def numbered_cabinet(c):
    for n in (1, 2):
        c.add(numbered_board, f"U{n}", name=f"module{n}")
    return Cabinet()


floating = fr.design("demo_parts")
floating.add(numbered_cabinet, "U1")
```

Check that the cabinet build has no errors.

```python
result = fr.build(d)
assert not [f for f in fr.check(result) if f.severity is fr.Severity.ERROR]
```

## Recording revisions

A unit's `revision=` only states which revision is current. Earlier entries go in `history=`, a
list of mappings with `revision`, `date`, `text` and `created`. The decorator writes the history
first, then the unit's own entry from `date=`, `text=` and `by=`. If the current revision has no
entry, the build reports `REVISION_CURRENT_MISSING`.
Each history entry also takes `version`. An entry with no `version` takes the unit's current
version, so after a version bump, earlier entries must name their old `version`.

```python
from typing import NamedTuple

class Io(NamedTuple):
    X1: fr.Device


@fr.unit(
    "demo-io-board",
    revision=2,
    interface_version=1,
    date="2026-02-02",
    text="added a spare connector",
    by="AB",
    history=[{"revision": 1, "date": "2026-01-01", "text": "first release", "created": "AB"}],
)
def board_r2(d):
    return Io(d.device("X1", "DEMO-CONN-2P", interface=True))


d = fr.design("demo_parts")
d.add(board_r2, "U1")
```

`d.revision(revision, date=, text=, created=)` writes one history entry of the project itself,
the same way, on a design that is not a unit.

`fr.release` refuses a history entry that names a revision never released, as
`RELEASE_HISTORY_UNRELEASED`. The cutoff is the first entry, in history order (date, then version
and revision), that names a released revision. Entries before it are free text, such as an old
register's. Each later entry needs a folder under `into` in its own version, or must be the revision
being released. A first release has no folders, so every entry is free. A system release checks the
project's history the same way.

## Writing one unit

`fr.write(result, out_dir, unit="demo-io-board")` restricts `out_dir` to that unit's own
documents and lists. A unit's release name is the `unit=` value. The tuple `d.add` returns, such as
`io`, is not accepted there. To list a model's units, read `sorted(fr.derive.units(model))`.

---

<!-- source: https://olejbondahl.github.io/fransys/0.23.5/guide/build/index.md -->

# Building a design

`fr.build`, `fr.check` and `fr.write` are the three pipeline functions. `build` takes the design
(and any documents), merges them into a model and runs the passes, the validators, and layout
when there is a document. `check` collects every finding about a built model, including some
`build` never sees. `write` writes the model's exports to a directory. If any finding is an
`ERROR` it raises `BuildFailedError`, writes no export, and removes the exports an earlier `write` left
there. `check` also places the system overview (`overview.html`) and returns its findings.
`settings=fr.settings(...)` sets the build's paper (settings.md).

`fr.__version__` gives the installed version. It is not in `fr.__all__`.

## Where a build can fail

Four stages, each failing differently. A design call the builder refuses raises `fr.AuthorError`
at that call.

**1. Loading a part library.** `fr.design(...)` and `fr.parts(...)` lint every library they load
and raise `PartLibraryError` if linting finds an `ERROR`. 

**2. The build itself.** `fr.build(d, *documents)` merges the design with the documents, then
freezes the result into a `Model`. Two structural problems can raise here.

- `MergeConflictError`, when two records share one id with different content. It can raise at the second authoring call that creates the record.
- `FreezeError`, when freezing finds one or more structural problems inside the merged records: a
  dangling reference, a bad value, or a missing required field. It aggregates every problem it
  found in `.errors`, so an author fixes a batch in one pass.

A consumer meets this with two instances of one unit release authored with different content.

```python
from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr


class Io(NamedTuple):
    X1: fr.Device


@fr.unit("demo-io-board", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-09-27", text="First", by="OJB")
def board_a(d):
    return Io(d.device("X1", "DEMO-CONN-2P", interface=True))


@fr.unit("demo-io-board", revision=1, interface_version=2, date="2026-09-27", text="First", by="OJB")
def board_b(d):
    return Io(d.device("X1", "DEMO-CONN-2P", interface=True))


conflict_design = fr.design("demo_parts")
conflict_design.add(board_a, "U1")

try:
    conflict_design.add(board_b, "U2")
except fr.MergeConflictError as e:
    assert "two different records share one id" in str(e)
    assert e.origin_a.file == e.origin_b.file
    assert e.origin_a.line != e.origin_b.line
else:
    raise AssertionError("expected MergeConflictError")
```

Both declare the release `demo-io-board`, revision 1, but with a different `interface`, so they
conflict instead of deduplicating. `e.origin_a` and `e.origin_b` name the call sites.

`fr.build(d)` always carries the design's part library. Only `d.draft()` leaves it out; building
that shows what a missing library does.

```python
d = fr.design("demo_parts")
x1 = d.device("X1", "DEMO-CONN-2P")

try:
    fr.build(d.draft())  # the authored records without the library
except fr.FreezeError as e:
    assert len(e.errors) == 4
else:
    raise AssertionError("expected FreezeError")
```

The missing library leaves four references dangling, one `RefError` each. `e.errors` holds all four.

Any other exception out of `build` is a Fransys bug. Report it as a field case.

**3. The validators.** Every domain validator runs inside `build`, but an `ERROR` finding from
one of them does not raise. It comes back in `fr.check(result)` and stops layout: the model is returned numbered but unlaid.

**4. `write`.** `write` computes `fr.check(result)` itself and raises `BuildFailedError` if any
finding in it is an `ERROR`, before touching `out_dir`. See below.

## `fr.check(result)` is the one list of findings

`fr.check(result)` returns every finding about a built model: the PLC and numbering passes, the
validators, layout and the board check, plus the drawing and PDF checks when it holds a document.

A cabinet with no device in it has nothing to draw. Its document holds the preset's pages, and
its empty lists are reported:

```python
from pathlib import Path

cabinet_cover = Path("cabinet.md")
cabinet_cover.write_text("# Cabinet\n")
c1 = d.location("C1", "Cabinet")
doc = fr.document(fr.DocumentPreset.CABINET_SCHEMATIC, c1, cover=cabinet_cover)

result = fr.build(d, doc)
assert len(fr.check(result)) == 5
```

`fr.check(result)` holds four `DOCUMENT_EMPTY_LIST` `INFO` findings and one `ERROR`, `DOCUMENT_NO_DRAWINGS`,
that only the drawing and PDF checks find. The cabinet holds nothing, so the document has no drawing.

`write` runs the same check internally, so it raises on those errors:

```python
try:
    fr.write(result, Path("out"))
except fr.BuildFailedError as e:
    assert len(e.findings) == 1
    assert all(f.severity is fr.Severity.ERROR and f.fix for f in e.findings)
else:
    raise AssertionError("no error")
```

`e.findings` holds only the `ERROR` findings. `out_dir` is left with nothing written for this build.
`write` has no `allow_errors`, `force` or `draft` parameter.

## `fr.report(result)` prints them for a person or an agent

`fr.report(result)` returns one text of `fr.check(result)`. Its first line counts the errors,
warnings and notes. Each `ERROR` and `WARNING` follows with its message, one `at:` line per
subject (the authoring call's `file:line`), its fix, and its row's URL. The notes come last,
counted per code on one line.

```python
text = fr.report(result)
assert text.startswith("build: 1 error, 0 warnings, 4 notes\n")
assert "  see: https://olejbondahl.github.io/fransys/" in text
assert "/guide/findings-pdf/#document_no_drawings\n" in text
assert text.endswith("notes: DOCUMENT_EMPTY_LIST 4\n")
```

The fix and the URL come from the code's row in [`findings.md`](https://olejbondahl.github.io/fransys/0.23.5/guide/findings/index.md). Print the report on every build.

## Which route carries which finding

| route | carries | when you read it |
|---|---|---|
| `result.findings` | What `fr.build` collected: the PLC and numbering passes, the validators and layout. | After `fr.build`. |
| `fr.check(result)` | `result.findings` plus the KiCad, PDF and render checks, errors first. | Any time after `fr.build`. |
| `fr.report(result)` | The text of `fr.check(result)`, with each fix and the URL of its findings row. | Any time after `fr.build`. |
| `fr.BuildFailedError.findings` | The `ERROR` findings of the `fr.write` or `fr.release` run that raised. `fr.release` adds its checks. | When the call raises. |

## No document, no layout

Layout exists only to draw documents. A build with no `Document` draft skips layout; there is no flag.

```python
result = fr.build(d)  # no document this time
codes = sorted(f.code for f in fr.check(result))
assert codes == []

written = fr.write(result, Path("out"))
assert sorted(p.relative_to("out").as_posix() for p in written) == [
    "data/bom.csv",
    "data/cables.csv",
    "data/cores.csv",
    "data/designations.csv",
    "data/plc.csv",
    "data/wires.csv",
    "overview.html",
]
```

`fr.export_names(result, *, unit=None)` gives the name `write` gives each export, by `(kind, subject)`,
writing nothing. A kind is `bom`, `plc`, `wires`, `designations`, `overview`,
`cables`, `cores`, `terminals` or `connectors` (subject `None`); `wago` with the rack's id; `pdf` or `ring_out` with the document's id. The key is a tuple: `("bom", None)` for a whole-set file, `("pdf", <document id>)`
for a document.

```python
names = fr.export_names(result)
assert names[("bom", None)] == "data/bom.csv"
assert [key for key in names if key[0] == "pdf"] == []  # no document: no ("pdf", id) key
assert sorted(names.values()) == sorted(p.relative_to("out").as_posix() for p in written)
```

With no document, `check` runs no drawing or PDF checks, and `write` writes no PDF.

## Export file names

One function builds every export name, so a script never constructs its own. The `v` prefix
appears only in file names, never in a title block or history table. The names have no option or template.

- **The set prefix.** Every file belongs to one set: the unit written (`unit=U`) or the
  system (`unit=None`). The prefix is `<set name>-v<V>.<R>`, the set's name plus its version and
  revision in `derive.revision_text`'s print form. A unit's name is its release name
  (`demo-io-board-v1.1`); the system's is the project's number (`EX-1-v1.1`). A system write of
  a model with no project record has no prefix: its own files keep bare names (`bom.csv`).
- **Prefix, kind, fragment.** A name is `<prefix>[-<kind>][-<fragment>].<ext>`:
  `demo-io-board-v1.1-bom.csv`, and per PLC rack `demo-io-board-v1.1-wago-U1.xml`.
- **Lists.** `terminals.csv` holds every strip, `connectors.csv` every board.
- **Where each list is.** A unit's cables stay in its own `cables.csv`; a parent sees the unit as a black box.
- **A PDF is named by its subject, not its cover file.** The set's own document is
  `<prefix>.pdf`. A document of an item or location inside
  the set adds that subject's fragment. A document whose subject is a unit takes that unit's
  name in every write, so `out/all/` holds `EX-1-v1.1.pdf` beside `cabinet-v2.1.pdf`. A whole-model write adds each placement's instance tag
  (`cabinet-v2.1-P1.pdf`); a unit's own write names its PDF bare. Untagged instances of one release clash.
- **The `data/` folder.** Every CSV and XML export goes into `<out_dir>/data/`, `changes.csv` included;
  the PDFs, `overview.html` and `changes.md` stay in `out_dir`. `fr.export_names` gives the path from `out_dir` (`data/EX-1-v1.1-bom.csv`).
- **Stale exports.** `write` first deletes the set's old files in `out_dir` and `data/`. These are files whose names start
  with the set's name and `-v`, and the flat CSV and XML files a write made before `data/` existed.
  A system write also deletes the files that start with each unit release's name and `-v`.
  The old bare-name patterns are still cleaned for one more release. Known limit: a unit that leaves the model leaves its last PDF in `out/all/`.
- **Build times.** `result.times` holds the CPU and wall seconds of each build step, and `print(result.times)` shows one line per step with its CPU share. With `intermediates=`, `write` also saves `build-times.json` there; `out_dir` never holds it.
- **Releases.** `fr.release` writes the same paths, and its manifest lists them (`data/...`).
  A release stored before `data/` keeps its flat paths and still verifies.
- **Changes in the overview.** `fr.write(result, out_dir, releases=into)` takes the folder you pass
  to `fr.release`. When it holds a release of the system (at the model's revision, else the previous), `overview.html` gains a Changes switch that marks what changed since it.
  Without `releases`, or with no release there, the page has no such switch.

Every file `write` writes is UTF-8 without a byte order mark, with `\n` line ends, on every OS.

## No export ever carries an error

Any `ERROR` in `fr.check(result)` blocks every export into `out_dir`. A half-finished design
still draws its schematic pages into `intermediates`, when given.

## Releasing a frozen baseline

`fr.release(result, into, *, unit=None)` writes one unit's (or the whole system's) frozen
baseline. It has its document set, as `write` would for that unit, plus a canonical
listing, a manifest of file hashes and package/tool versions, and the model itself. The target
is `<into>/<unit release name>/<version>.<revision>/`, or `<into>/<project number>/<version>.<revision>/`
for the system (`unit=None`). Every check runs first -- the same gate `write` uses,
plus five checks of its own -- and any `ERROR` writes nothing.

```python
def board(revision, *, spare=None):
    """One unit design: the release `demo-io-board`, X1 on its boundary, X3, an optional spare."""

    @fr.unit(
        "demo-io-board", revision=revision, interface_version=1, date="2026-09-27", text=f"Revision {revision}", by="OJB"
    )
    def io_board(d):
        x1 = d.device("X1", "DEMO-CONN-2P", interface=True)
        d.device("X3", "DEMO-CONN-2P")
        if spare:
            d.device(spare, "DEMO-CONN-2P")
        return Io(x1)

    release_design = fr.design("demo_parts")
    release_design.add(io_board, "U1")
    return release_design


release_result = fr.build(board(1))
release_errors = [f for f in fr.check(release_result) if f.severity is fr.Severity.ERROR]
assert release_errors == [], release_errors

target = fr.release(release_result, Path("releases"), unit="demo-io-board")
assert target == Path("releases") / "demo-io-board" / "1.1"
assert (target / "baseline" / "listing.json").exists()
assert (target / "baseline" / "manifest.json").exists()

# releasing the same, unchanged model again writes nothing new
same_target = fr.release(release_result, Path("releases"), unit="demo-io-board")
assert same_target == target
```

An unchanged release is a no-op. A released
revision is frozen: releasing a unit again with different content raises `BuildFailedError` naming
`REVISION_ALREADY_RELEASED` instead of overwriting it (see `findings-validators.md`). Commit the files in your own repo, beside the design script.

A container rebuilt against an old child release uses the child's old source from git. Fransys loads no frozen child.
A history entry that names a revision never released is `RELEASE_HISTORY_UNRELEASED`; `units.md` has the rule.

## Getting the change list

`fr.diff(result, into, *, unit=None, against=None)` gives the Markdown change list from a
stored release to the model as it stands now, without writing anything: use it during a revision. `release()` writes the same text into `changes.md` (and the same rows
into `data/changes.csv`) once a previous release exists; the first release of a unit gets neither
file. Nothing overwrites the history text you author. A unit's change list is relative to the unit, so a place that holds all of its items, added or removed, shows no change.

```python
second_result = fr.build(board(2, spare="X2"))
second_errors = [f for f in fr.check(second_result) if f.severity is fr.Severity.ERROR]
assert second_errors == [], second_errors

preview = fr.diff(second_result, Path("releases"), unit="demo-io-board")
assert "Added `-X2`" in preview

second_target = fr.release(second_result, Path("releases"), unit="demo-io-board")
assert (second_target / "changes.md").read_text(encoding="utf-8") == preview
assert (second_target / "data" / "changes.csv").exists()
```

`against=` names a released revision's folder (`"1.1"`) to diff against. The default is the model's
own release if stored, else the previous one; `fr.diff` raises `FileNotFoundError` when neither exists. A renamed item shows as one `Renamed` line; `moving-to-0.20.md` has the rule.

## Checking a baseline stays true

`fr.verify(result, baselines) -> tuple[Finding, ...]` reruns `release`'s `BASELINE_DIFFERS`
comparison for every unit instance (and the system, when the model has a project) with a stored
baseline. It writes nothing, and `fr.write` never calls it: run it in a test that guards a released revision.

```python
assert fr.verify(second_result, Path("releases")) == ()

third_result = fr.build(board(2, spare="X9"))  # X2, mistagged X9
third_errors = [f for f in fr.check(third_result) if f.severity is fr.Severity.ERROR]
assert third_errors == [], third_errors

findings = fr.verify(third_result, Path("releases"))
assert [f.code for f in findings] == ["BASELINE_DIFFERS"]
```

`second_result` is unchanged since its release, so `verify` gives nothing. `third_result` shares
revision `2` but its spare connector's tag differs from what `1.2` released, so `verify` catches
the drift. A unit with no stored baseline is not reported.

When a child moved release, `BASELINE_DIFFERS` names it right after `units`, as in
`demo-cabinet 1.1 differs from its released baseline in: units (demo-io-board revision 1.1 → 1.3)`.
It names direct children only; a grandchild's move shows in its parent's finding.

`verify` also re-hashes every release file under `baselines`, with no model needed.
`RELEASE_FILE_CHANGED` means a listed file's bytes differ, an unlisted file is present, or the manifest does not parse. `RELEASE_FILE_MISSING` means a listed file, or the manifest, is gone.
A text file (`.csv`, `.json`, `.md`, `.xml`, `.html`, `.txt`) whose bytes differ only by CRLF line ends passes,
so a Windows checkout passes.

After an upgrade that moved a printing rule, `fr.verify` gives `BASELINE_RULES_MOVED_NOTE` (INFO) for each release cut by an older Fransys and `fr.release` refuses over one. Run `fr.rebaseline(result, Path("releases"))` once and commit the rewritten `listing.json` and `manifest.json`; the exports are untouched.

```python
found = fr.verify(second_result, Path("releases"))
if any(f.code.startswith(("BASELINE_RULES_MOVED", "BASELINE_ROWS_UNCHECKED")) for f in found):
    fr.rebaseline(second_result, Path("releases"))  # commit the rewritten baseline files
assert fr.verify(second_result, Path("releases")) == ()
```

A patch release reads every revision; rebaseline only on `BASELINE_RULES_MOVED_NOTE`.

## Listing the releases

`fr.releases(root) -> tuple[Release, ...]` reads every `<name>/<version>.<revision>/` folder under
`root`, in name, version and revision order. Versions and revisions sort as integers. A
`Release` has `name`, `version`, `revision`, `interface`, `listing_digest`, `nested`, `files` and `path`.
`nested` holds one `ReleasePin` (`name`, `version`, `revision`, `listing_digest`) per release nested
in it. `files` holds `(path, sha256)` pairs. A folder with no manifest is listed with empty fields.
A manifest that does not parse raises `ValueError`.

Later versions may add manifest keys and keep reading every earlier manifest.

```python
listed = fr.releases(Path("releases"))
assert [(r.name, r.version, r.revision) for r in listed] == [
    ("demo-io-board", 1, 1),
    ("demo-io-board", 1, 2),
]
assert listed[0].interface == "1"

# Which parents to bump: a release whose pin of a child is older than the child's latest release.
latest = {r.name: (r.version, r.revision) for r in listed}
stale = [
    (r.name, f"{r.version}.{r.revision}", pin.name)
    for r in listed
    for pin in r.nested
    if latest.get(pin.name) not in (None, (pin.version, pin.revision))
]
assert stale == []
```

The policy stays yours: tag names, who releases and which findings block. Fransys keeps no issue record.

## Keeping designations fixed across revisions

`fr.build(d, *documents, releases=None)` takes a keyword-only `releases`, the same root `fr.release`
writes into. At `None` (the default), numbering is free. Given the releases root, `build` reads each unit's
released numbering before assigning new tags. An item still in the same group keeps the number it was released with. A number
freed by a removed or moved item is never handed to a different item within that unit's
version. An authored tag that equals a pinned or reserved number is `DESIGNATION_DUPLICATE`
(see `findings-build.md`). Releasing without
`releases=` still catches a moved number, as `DESIGNATION_MOVED`.

## Point a finding past a helper

A finding names the file and line of the call that authored the thing. Set `__tracebackhide__ = True`
in a helper that builds a repeated circuit, and the finding names the helper's caller.

```python
import fransys as fr


def lamp_pair(d, first, second):
    __tracebackhide__ = True
    return d.device(first, "DEMO-LAMP-24"), d.device(second, "DEMO-LAMP-24")


d = fr.design("demo_parts")
h1, h2 = lamp_pair(d, "H1", "H2")
result = fr.build(d)
assert fr.derive.item_designation(result.model, h1.id) == "H1"
```

## Read a model id

`Q1.id` and `Q1.coil.id` give the model id of a device and a function. Read them after the build, as
`fr.derive.item_designation(result.model, Q1.id)` does. Never wire with ids.

---

<!-- source: https://olejbondahl.github.io/fransys/0.23.5/guide/documents/index.md -->

# Documents

A `Document` record is what turns an authored design into a printable deliverable. `fr.document`
authors one such record as a `Draft`. Pass it to `fr.build(d, doc)` next to the design `d`;
the model does the rest at layout and write time.

## Presets, cover and notes text

`fr.document(preset, subject, cover=..., logo=None, notice="")` takes a
`fr.DocumentPreset` (`CABINET_SCHEMATIC` or `SYSTEM`), which fixes the deliverable's page kinds.
`cover` is a required path to a Markdown file, read verbatim and stored on the model; any number of documents may share one cover path. A
missing `cover` is a `FileNotFoundError` naming the path. A file beside it, named the cover's
stem plus `.notes.md`, is read automatically when present and becomes the document's notes
page. There is no separate `notes` parameter. A missing notes file is not an error; it just
means no notes page. `logo` is an optional path to an SVG for the title block's logo cell, read the same way; leaving it out (the
default) leaves that cell empty. `notice` is the text of the title block's IP notice cell, printed
on every page of that document; `""` (the default) leaves the cell empty. On A3 the cell is about 92 mm wide and holds about 370 characters at the label size. A longer notice gives `TITLE_BLOCK_NOTICE_OVERFLOW`. Customer and Author are narrower than with no notice. A unit released alone
needs no `d.project` for either; its Author cell prints `created` of the unit's current revision, a project document's the project's `author`. `d.project(notice=...)` raises: the notice moved here.

The page kinds each preset holds, in the order of the PDF: the cover, the drawings, then the notes, the index and the lists. The cover is page 1 and the drawings start on page 2.

| page kind | `CABINET_SCHEMATIC` | `SYSTEM` |
|---|---|---|
| `COVER` | yes | yes |
| `BLOCK_DIAGRAM` | no | yes |
| `SCHEMATIC` | yes | no |
| `HARNESS_DRAWING` | no | yes |
| `NOTES` | yes | yes |
| `SHEET_INDEX` | yes | yes |
| `PLC_LIST` | yes | no |
| `TERMINAL_LIST` | yes | no |
| `CONNECTOR_LIST` | yes | no |
| `CABLE_LIST` | no | yes |
| `BOM` | yes | yes |

Every preset also takes `PageKind.SHEET_INDEX`, a "Sheets" page after the notes that lists each
drawing page with its title and its PDF page. It prints from two pages. The PDF is navigable and
prints the same. Cross references and Sheets rows are invisible links. The outline lists pages and
devices. A page has one number: its place in its PDF, counted from 1 with the cover as page 1. Every reference,
the Sheets page, the outline and the viewer print it. The title block prints it as `m of N`, with the
PDF's page count.

```python
from pathlib import Path
from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BK



class Cabinet(NamedTuple):
    pass


@fr.unit(
    "terminal-cabinet",
    revision=1,
    interface_version=1,
    date="2026-02-02",
    text="First",
    by="XX",
    title="Terminal cabinet",
    number="TC-1",
)
def terminal_cabinet(c):
    x1 = c.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 2, description="Field strip")
    f1 = c.device("F1", "DEMO-FUSE-ABAT")
    c.series(x1, f1.element, x1, wire=(BK, 1.5))
    return Cabinet()


d = fr.design("demo_parts")
d.add(terminal_cabinet, "U1")

cover = Path("cabinet.md")
cover.write_text("# Cabinet\n", encoding="utf-8")
Path("cabinet.notes.md").write_text("Site notes for the installer.\n", encoding="utf-8")

cabinet_document = fr.document(fr.DocumentPreset.CABINET_SCHEMATIC, "terminal-cabinet", cover=cover)
result = fr.build(d, cabinet_document)
findings = fr.check(result)
assert not [f for f in findings if f.severity in (fr.Severity.ERROR, fr.Severity.WARNING)]
written = fr.write(result, Path("out"))
assert any(p.suffix == ".pdf" for p in written)
```

`out/` now holds one PDF for the cabinet, with the cover and notes text on their own pages
ahead of the schematic.

## Subjects

A document's `subject` is a unit, an item, or a place where units stand. It is one of:

- A location handle, what `d.location(...)` returns: a place where units stand.
- A device handle, what `d.device(...)` or `d.harness(...)` returns.
- A unit release's name, a plain `str`, such as a cabinet's: resolved to the one instance of that release at build
  and write time, not at the `fr.document` call itself.
- What `d.add(...)` returned: that one unit instance. Use it when a release stands more than once, since a name
  then matches several units and `DOCUMENT_UNIT_UNRESOLVED` follows.

Any other value, such as a bare design, is a `TypeError` at the call. The cabinet example above
passes its release name. A unit added with `d.add(fn, "U1")` is named by its release name:

```python
class Io(NamedTuple):
    X1: fr.Device


@fr.unit("demo-io-board", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-02-02", text="First", by="XX")
def board(u):
    x1 = u.device("X1", "DEMO-CONN-2P", interface=True)
    x2 = u.terminal_strip("X2", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 3)
    h1 = u.device("H1", "DEMO-LAMP-24")
    u.series(x2, h1.lamp, x2, wire=(BK, 0.5))
    return Io(x1)


d2 = fr.design("demo_parts")
d2.add(board, "U1")
board_document = fr.document(fr.DocumentPreset.CABINET_SCHEMATIC, "demo-io-board", cover=cover)
board_result = fr.build(d2, board_document)
assert not [f for f in fr.check(board_result) if f.severity is fr.Severity.ERROR]
assert any(p.name == "demo-io-board-v1.1.pdf" for p in fr.write(board_result, Path("out1")))
```

The PDF is named after the unit and its release, `demo-io-board-v1.1.pdf`.

What `d.add` returned names its instance, so a document can follow the instance rather than the release name:

```python
d3 = fr.design("demo_parts")
placed = d3.add(board, "U1")
placed_document = fr.document(fr.DocumentPreset.CABINET_SCHEMATIC, placed, cover=cover)
placed_result = fr.build(d3, placed_document)
assert not [f for f in fr.check(placed_result) if f.severity is fr.Severity.ERROR]
```

A release added more than once resolves by name to no single unit. Name each instance by what `d.add` returned. Each placement writes its own PDF, `<release>-v<V>.<R>-<tag>.pdf`; the unit's own PDF stays `<release>-v<V>.<R>.pdf`.

## List pages

The terminal, PLC, connector, wire-label and designation lists flow in two columns. The cable list and the BOM take the full width. A row never splits. A table that reaches a column foot continues in the next column or page under its heading with " (cont.)". A split leaves at least two rows on each side, else the table moves whole. A long token breaks only at a hyphen or a slash. The cover's revision table stands one padding above the title block.

The connector list prints one table per connector, headed by its designation and the item's description, with a row per pin: Pin, Net, Mate and Ends. The `CABINET_SCHEMATIC` preset carries it. A pin no wire inside the unit reaches is not drawn on the unit's own pages, and its row in the connector table is where it shows. A cabinet document with no connector reports an INFO `DOCUMENT_EMPTY_LIST`, as it does for terminals.

## Cable drawings

A `HARNESS_DRAWING` page draws each cable as one block, and a harness of two or more cables as one block around its cables. A block has its end boxes with their pins, a box per cable with its heading, and one wire per core. A core whose two ends stand in one row is a short link at that row. Two cores on one pin stand side by side in the pin's cell. A harness whose cables interleave is not drawn yet. A document that shows it stops with
`DOCUMENT_NO_DRAWINGS`.

A `TERMINAL_LIST` page lists the terminal strips of each unit and location. A document whose design has no unit and no location lists nothing, so declare a unit or a location to get the page.

## Block diagrams

A `BLOCK_DIAGRAM` page draws a reading as boxes joined by one line per cable. The line carries the
cable's designation, and a tab names the strip or connector it lands on. The `SYSTEM` preset
carries the page after the notes: its boxes are the top-level units and items, its lines the
top-level cables. A `CABINET_SCHEMATIC` document does not carry it. A reading with no cable line
gets no page.

The page is A2 landscape, 594 x 420 mm, with a 12 x 8 frame; the other pages keep the
document's sheet. A diagram wider than one sheet continues on the next, and a line cut between
sheets ends in a marker naming the other sheet. A kept page whose diagram cannot be drawn stops the
export with `DOCUMENT_NO_DRAWINGS`.

## One PDF is one drawing

Each `fr.document(...)` call, and each resulting PDF, is one drawing: a cabinet schematic, a
harness drawing, or a PCB schematic, never several combined into one file. A unit follows the
same rule at the unit's own level: a unit is one physical thing in one place, so its own items
make one drawing set. **A unit's drawings take the unit as subject; an item inside a unit is not a
drawing.** Places only split drawing sets at the top level, outside any unit.

Concretely: naming the unit's release (as `"demo-io-board"` above) draws that unit's one
schematic. Naming a device that sits inside a unit (`X1`, not the unit) matches no
drawing set at all. That is because its layout belongs to the unit, not
to the bare device. A schematic with nothing to draw adds no page and no finding while
the document has another content page (a list with rows, a harness drawing, a block diagram).
With none, `check` reports `DOCUMENT_NO_DRAWINGS` (an `ERROR`), and `write`
turns any `ERROR` into `fr.BuildFailedError` with no export written. The harness and diagram messages
of `DOCUMENT_NO_DRAWINGS` stay `ERROR`s whatever else the document holds.


The fix is never to add pages or merge drawings by hand: name the unit's release as the
document's subject, as the unit example on this page does.

---

<!-- source: https://olejbondahl.github.io/fransys/0.23.5/guide/reading/index.md -->

# Reading a model

`fransys.derive` is the read side of a model: every designation, table, row and rating a
script might need already has a function here. Layout, render and every output call the
same ones. Every function's docstring is its full reference. What follows is a short tour of the
read surface: enough to know what is there and how to reach for it.

Two facts hold across the whole surface:

- Ids are opaque keys. A script looks a record up by its id (in a table, or by passing the id
  to a `derive` function); it never builds, parses or prints an id itself.
- An item's name is `item.key[-1]`. There is no separate `.name` field.

## The tables

`fransys.derive.units(model)` returns every `Unit` of `model` as a
`frozendict[Id[Unit], Unit]`. The other tables follow the same shape: one function per record kind, keyed by id.

- `fransys.derive.nets(model)`: every `Net` of `model`, by id.
- `fransys.derive.unit_releases(model)`: every `UnitRelease` of `model`, by id. A
  `UnitRelease` is the product a `Unit` instantiates (its name, version, revision, interface,
  title and document number); several `Unit`s can share one release.
- `fransys.derive.supply_systems(model)`: every `SupplySystem` of `model`, by id. A
  `SupplySystem` is a declared supply and its rails (a potential name, its maximum voltage and,
  for AC, its phase).

## One unit's release

`fransys.derive.unit_release(model, unit)` reads the one `UnitRelease` record a `Unit`
instance is of. It is the one reader of a unit's release facts.

`fransys.derive.unit_location(model, unit)` returns the location node `unit` is placed at:
its root items' own location, or their nearest common ancestor; `None` when no root is placed.

`fransys.derive.unit_parent(model, unit)` returns the id of `unit`'s parent unit; `None` for a root.

`fransys.derive.location_texts(model)` returns each location label with its printed designation.

`fransys.derive.project_facts(model)` returns the title block's six facts of the project, as
`(title, number, customer, revision, revision_date, author)`; all are empty with no `Project`.

`fransys.derive.document_facts(model, document)` takes the document id and returns the same six facts:
a unit document's are its unit release's own, with `customer` empty and `author` the `created`
of the unit's current revision. Any other document's are the project's.

## Rails, boundaries and function kinds

`fransys.derive.port_rails(model, port)` returns the rails a port carries, as a
`frozenset[str]` of potential names: empty for a port that carries none, or is not in
`model`. A rail only exists once some `SupplySystem` declares the potential and some `Net`
carries it; wiring alone declares no rail.

`fransys.derive.port_potential_rank(model, port)` is the rank of the potential a pin carries, or `None`.
A smaller rank is drawn higher up. It reads the supply's facts, never a rail's name. The order is AC phases,
DC above 0 V, AC at 0 V, DC at 0 V, DC below 0 V, then PE. A pin behind a switch keeps its
rail's rank. A pin reached from two rails takes the lower. `fransys.derive.port_potential_current(model,
port)` gives the rail's `Current`, and `None` for PE or no rank.

`takes_energy(model, function)` is `True` when `function` takes energy in: its part's
declared `energy` when it has one, else `True` for a `load`, `actuator` or `coil`, else `False`.
A box draws the pins of an energy-in function above those of an energy-out one.

`gives_energy(model, function)` is `True` when `function` gives energy out: its part's
declared `energy` when it has one, else `True` for a `supply`, else `False`. A box draws
a function that takes or gives energy above a signal function.

`no_conductor_at(model, port)` is `True` when no conductor (wire, jumper, cable core
or link) ends at `port`. Unlike `unconnected_ports`, a mate or a declared net does not count.


`port_is_unused(model, port)` is `True` when no conductor ends at `port` and no declared
net has it. A mate does not count. `function_is_unused(model, function)` is `True` when
every port of `function` is unused: the function `hide_unused_pins` leaves off the page, and a contact
among them is a spare in its coil's contact table. `function_is_idle_terminal(model, function)` is `True` for a terminal no wire inside its drawing reaches.
`function_scopes(model, function)` returns the `(unit, place)` sets that draw `function`: its own, then each set holding a copy of a terminal.

`power_kind(model, net)` returns a `PowerKind` for a declared net: `SUPPLY`,
`GROUND`, `PE` or `NONE`. A net of class `pe` is `PE`. A potential of a DC supply is `GROUND` at
0 V and `SUPPLY` otherwise. An AC rail, a potential in no supply, no potential, or two
potentials on one wired net is `NONE`. So is a wired net of exactly two ports. A point-to-point
connection is a wire; only a net of three or more ports is a rail. A PE net stays `PE`. `port_power_kind(model, port)` gives the kind of a
port's wired net. A DC supply declares its 0 V rail (`rails={"24V": ("24", None), "0V": ("0",
None)}`). Without it, the 0 V net gets references, not a ground symbol. `power_text(model, net)`
is the text a power symbol prints. It is the supply's name, else its potential, then the tag of the nearest protective device the net lies behind (`24V -F2`). It is `None` for
`GROUND`, `PE` and `NONE`. `port_power_text(model, port)` gives the text of the symbol at a port.
`is_rail_terminal(model, terminal)` is true for a terminal in a group flagged `rail=True`.
A flagged terminal draws as its power symbol, an unflagged one as a terminal. A pin wired to one, or to another pin on a power net, draws the rail's power symbol. No wire joins two such pins. The terminal table and wire list hold every landing and wire.
A terminal is drawn at the pin it serves, once per page. So is a single-wire contact or a coil on a PLC output channel, with a reference back to its device. A rail symbol faces away from its box: up above a top pin, down below a bottom pin.
A terminal with no wire on a page is not drawn there. One wired to nothing is only in the terminal list.

`fransys.derive.wire_rows(model, *, unit=None)` returns the wire list: one `WireRow` per
wire, with `from_`, `to`, `colour`, `cross_section_mm2` and `ends`. The `ends` are the two end
designations joined by one space in a fixed order, the text the wire list and sleeves print. A schematic page prints no wire label.
`fr.write` writes these rows as `<set>-wires.csv`.

`fransys.derive.boundary(model, unit)` returns the functions that make up a unit's
interface, as a tuple of function ids in id order. A function of any kind can be a unit's boundary.

`fransys.derive.FunctionKind` is the enum of what a `Function` exposes: `COIL`,
`CONTACT_NO`, `TERMINAL`, `CONNECTOR`, `SUPPLY`, and so on. A function's `kind` is one of
these.

`fransys.derive.connector_facets(model)` returns every `connector` facet, by the function
template it describes, as a `frozendict[Id[FunctionTemplate], ConnectorFacet]`.

## Rows

`fransys.derive.bom_lines(model, scope=None, *, without=())` returns the parts list, one `BomLine` per
installed, non-external part (by mpn, revision and part), or one line per nested unit when
`scope` is a unit. `scope` narrows what is counted. `None` is the whole model; an item id, that item's subtree; an aspect-node id, what is placed there. A unit id gives that unit's
own items and its directly nested units. And `fransys.derive.TOP_LEVEL` for items with no
unit plus one line per top-level unit. `without=` names items that an item, aspect-node or
whole-model scope leaves out; a unit or `TOP_LEVEL` scope ignores it. `TOP_LEVEL`'s type,
`fransys.derive.TopLevelScope`, is exported only for annotations.

`fransys.derive.NO_PLACE` is the text "N/A" a coil's contact table prints after the mark of a
contact no conductor reaches, not a page position.

`fransys.derive.bom_sort_key(model, item)` is the sort key `bom_lines` orders a line's
`designations` by: a terminal by its strip, group and index; any other item by its whole
designation. Every printed list sorts through
`fransys.derive` keys: designations in `natural_key` order, so `-K2` sorts before `-K10`.

`fransys.derive.is_cable(model, item)` returns whether `item` is a cable: whether its part
carries a `cable_product` facet (decision model-0108). `fransys.derive.cable_items(model)`
returns every such item, as a `frozenset[Id[Item]]`. Neither reads `item`'s `category` or
its `cable` facet (only the as-installed length). Every cable-selecting function
on this page (`harness_cables`, `top_level_cables`, `unit_cables`, `cable_list_rows`) reads
through one of these two, so none disagrees on what a cable is.

`fransys.derive.reading_cables(model, unit)` returns `unit`'s cables or the top-level ones.

`fransys.derive.is_plc_module(model, item)` returns whether `item`'s part has category
`PLC_MODULE`. A rack is an item with at least one such child, and `plc_rack_modules` lists them.

`fransys.derive.plc_tables(model, unit=None)` returns the PLC list as one `PlcTable` per controller or module, in the row order of `plc_channel_rows`.

`fransys.derive.unit_strips(model, unit)` and `fransys.derive.unit_boards(model, unit)`
return the terminal strips and the boards that `unit` owns directly, sorted by id, never those of
a unit nested in it.

`fransys.derive.mates(model)` returns one `MateRow` per `d.mate` in the model, at every level: a mate
on a board, and a plug mated to a unit's interface connector. A row holds the two mated functions (each a connector or terminal),
`a` and `b` in id order, and `a_designation` and `b_designation`, the text the connector
list prints. Rows sort by those two texts. Reach an item through the function. `connector_rows` covers
board connectors only.

`fransys.derive.terminal_items(model)` returns every item that carries a `terminal` facet, as a
`frozenset[Id[Item]]`. Select terminals through it, so no script rebuilds the set.

`fransys.derive.pin_order(marking, port)` returns the sort key of a pin: markings of decimal digits
first by value, the rest after by string (`1, 2, 10, A1`). The connector list, `harness_cables` and
the overview sort by it, and `fn.pins` follows it. Sort pins through it, so no script keeps a second order.

`fransys.derive.harness_wires(model, harness)` returns the `WireRow`s of the wires on the harness's plugs.

`fransys.derive.cable_list_rows(model, unit=None)` returns one `CableListRow` per top-level cable,
or per cable of `unit`, with its product facts. `from_label` is the first end's designation; `to_label` lists the others,
in end order, joined by `, `. An end on a device that prints its connectors as sub-parts names the
connector behind the designation (`+C1-A1-X1`).
`pairs` is the number of twisted pairs of the cable's product, `None` for a product without pairs,
and `fransys.derive.cores_text(core_count, pairs)` is the Cores cell: `2x2` for two pairs, else the count.

## Designations

`fransys.derive.item_designation(model, item)` renders an item's own printed label, such as
`K1`, or `U1-K1` for one nested inside a board.

`fransys.derive.port_designation(model, port)` renders a port's label: the item's
designation plus the port's name, dash-prefixed like every physical tag (`-K1:13`).

`fransys.derive.reference_designation(model, item)` renders an item's full reference: its
location and its product designation together (`+C1-K1`).

`fransys.derive.printed_designation(model, item)` renders an item the way a list prints it:
dash-prefixed, product part only, with no location segment.

Each of these takes further keyword-only options; their docstrings cover the exact rules.

`fransys.derive.item_label(model, item)` takes the item's id and is `item_designation`'s no-raise twin: an item's own
text, or its authoring key joined by `/` when it has none yet.

`fransys.derive.drawn_designations(model, ids)` gives the designation of each item whose id a drawing carries as text, such as `DrawnRow.devices`. See "Read the rows of a page" in the readability page.

`fransys.derive.node_designation(model, node)` renders a node's signed
designation by aspect: `+C1` for a location, `=G1` for a group. It is the segment
`reference_designation` prints for an item there. A title block's scope cell prints a location's full path,
such as `+R+S1`.


`fransys.derive.item_of_port(model, port)` returns the item whose function owns `port`, the
lookup `port_designation` itself reads through.

## Ratings

`fransys.derive.part_rating(model, part)` returns the rating stated on a part itself, for a
part with no function to rate, such as a fuse link. `None` when the part states none. It reads
the model after the build.
`d.rating` and `d.operating` state a rating or an operating envelope while authoring; the
functions below read it back.

`fransys.derive.function_rating(model, function)` returns the rating a function's template
states, else its part's. `None` when neither states one.

`fransys.derive.part_function_rows(model)` returns one `PartFunctionRow` per function a part
declares: its `part`, `mpn`, `template`, `name`, `kind` and `rating`, sorted by MPN. A part with
no function, such as a fuse link, has one row with `template` and `kind` `None` and `name`
empty. `rating` is the function's own, else the part's, the rule `function_rating` reads. It
needs no design: a parts-only build is enough.

`fransys.derive.function_operating(model, function)` returns the operating envelope a
function's template states. `None` with no template or no such facet.


## Checking a branch's current

`RATING_CURRENT_BELOW_BRANCH` compares each rated function with the current its branch can carry.
A branch is bounded by a full-range protective device's rated current and by a source's
`max_current` figure. A partial-range fuse, one with a minimum breaking current,
bounds nothing. A load's draw is not an input.

Every device on the branch must be rated at least the bound. Below it, the finding is an `ERROR`.
Here a 160 A fuse protects a branch of a 186 A source, and the contactor pole is rated 150 A.

```python
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BK

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
g1 = d.device("G1", "DEMO-STRING-864V")
f1 = d.device("F1", "DEMO-FUSE-DC-160")
k1 = d.device("K1", "DEMO-CONTACTOR-DC")
x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 2, external=True)
dc = d.dc_supply("HV", g1.string)
d.series(dc.plus, f1, k1, x1, wire=(BK, 1.5))
d.series(dc.minus, x1, wire=(BK, 1.5))

result = fr.build(d)
(finding,) = [f for f in fr.check(result) if f.code == "RATING_CURRENT_BELOW_BRANCH"]
assert finding.severity is fr.Severity.ERROR
```

`fr.derive.current_chains(model)` returns the rated paths, grouped by loop, in order from the supply
end. Each position names its functions and its bounds. A bound holds the value, the function that set
it and its role, `source` or `protection`. Here the fuse's 160 A is the smallest limit reaching the pole.

```python
bounds = {b for c in fr.derive.current_chains(result.model) for p in c.positions for b in p.bounds}
assert {(b.value, b.role.value) for b in bounds} == {(160, "protection")}
```

Not checked: isolation, a cable against its installation, busbar authoring, a through-hole sensor, and
per-path ratings across the functions of one part. A rated busbar item is checked like any other device.

## Checking a fault and a load

`RATING_BREAKING_BELOW_FAULT` compares a protective device's breaking points with the prospective fault
current at its position. `fr.derive.prospective_fault(model)` returns what it reads: one `ProspectiveFault`
per protective position and current kind. An entry holds the `position`, the `kind`, `current_a`,
`time_constant_ms`, and the source `functions` counted.

A source is a function that gives energy. A supply input takes energy and is no source. A source function with more than two conductive ports
counts as no source: its pins would have to be grouped by rail.

A bolted fault at one terminal of the device joins it to every other rail of the supplies the device
reaches. A DC fuse behind a power supply does not see the AC rails. The device carries the sources on
a path from the fault to its other terminal. A series run of sources counts at its largest member and
parallel runs add. The larger of the two terminals' values is the entry's.

The value is conservative only given every feed declared. Cable and busbar resistance are ignored, which
errs high. An undeclared feed counts as no source, which errs low, so state every source's fault current in its part file.
A position no source reaches reads `0`. A counted source that states none makes the value `None`, and the
check stays silent.

`LOAD_ABOVE_LIMIT` and `LOADS_ABOVE_LIMIT` compare a load's draw with the limit that bounds it.
`fr.derive.load_limits(model)` returns one `LoadLimit` per load edge: the `function`, the `port` of a
star edge (`None` for a two-port load), the `kind`, `draw_a` and the `bound`. The `bound` is a
`CurrentBound`, or `None` when no limit bounds the load. The draw is the part's `nominal_current_a`,
as stated.

## A worked example

The design is authored with `fr.design`; every read below runs on `result.model` after the build.
A pin handle such as `housing[1]` has an `.id`; an item is found by its `tag` in
`fr.derive.items(model)`.

```python
from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BK, BN


class Io(NamedTuple):
    P1: fr.Device


@fr.unit("power-tap", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-09-26", text="First", by="XX")
def power_tap(u):
    return Io(u.device("P1", "DEMO-CONN-2P", interface=True))


d = fr.design("demo_parts")
housing = d.device("X10", "DEMO-CONN-2P")
cable = d.cable("W1", "DEMO-CBL-4G1.5", length_m=2)
loose = d.device("X11", "DEMO-CONN-2P")
cable.core(BN, housing[1], loose[1])
cable.core(BK, loose[2], d.add(power_tap, "U1").P1[1])

supply = d.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24")
dc = d.dc_supply("main", supply)
x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 1)
d.series(dc.plus, x1, wire=(BN, 0.75))

result = fr.build(d)  # no document: no layout
model = result.model
ids = {item.tag: item.id for item in fr.derive.items(model).values() if item.tag}

(unit_id,) = fr.derive.units(model)
release = fr.derive.unit_release(model, unit_id)
assert release.name == "power-tap"

(boundary_function,) = fr.derive.boundary(model, unit_id)
assert fr.derive.functions(model)[boundary_function].kind is fr.derive.FunctionKind.CONNECTOR

assert fr.derive.port_rails(model, x1[1].inner.id) == frozenset({"24V"})
assert fr.derive.nets(model)
assert len(fr.derive.bom_lines(model)) == 4  # connector, cable, supply, terminal
assert len(fr.derive.cable_list_rows(model)) == 1
assert len(fr.derive.contents_rows(fr.derive.top_level_cables(model))) == 1
assert fr.derive.printed_designation(model, ids["X11"]) == "-X11"

cable_part = fr.derive.items(model)[ids["W1"]].part
assert cable_part is not None
cable_rating = fr.derive.part_rating(model, cable_part)
assert cable_rating is not None and cable_rating.voltage[0].nom == fr.elecdef.Unit.V(500)
```

---

<!-- source: https://olejbondahl.github.io/fransys/0.23.5/guide/layout-numbers/index.md -->

# Layout numbers

This page lists every keyword of `d.layout.profile`: what it does, its house value, its effect on the drawing, and when to change it.
A gap is in grid units `G`; eight `G` make one symbol module.

## Sheet

A document's sheet is set for the whole build with `fr.settings(paper=...)` and `paper_by_kind` (see settings.md): A3 or A2, landscape. No call of a design or a unit sets or changes a sheet.

## Profile keywords

`d.layout.profile(...)` sets the layout numbers of the design, or of the unit whose body calls it. At most one per unit. A keyword left out keeps its house value. A value given replaces it whole. A unit with no profile uses the house values, never its parent's. `d.layout.profile` does not draw anything: it advises the layout engine.

| keyword | house value | what it does | effect on the drawing | when to change it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `hide_unused_pins` | `False` | Hide a box-drawn pin with no conductor, and a function with none, on drawings only. | Drawings are shorter; every list still shows every pin. A box in a chain draws only its wired pins (LONG-CHAIN D2). | An interface with many unused pins. |

## Grid pitch and printed sizes

`module_mm` sets the grid pitch and must equal the library's 2.5: symbols never scale. A crowded page is never fixed by size. Split the content into function blocks (`drawing.md`). A well-formed design that still overflows is a Fransys defect: send the smallest model.
The text sizes are the library's fixed heights, not a profile keyword and not a setting. Never use the text size to make a page fit: a page that is too full needs less on the page, split into function blocks.

---

<!-- source: https://olejbondahl.github.io/fransys/0.23.5/guide/reading-rows/index.md -->

# Reading: rows, columns and printed texts

This page covers `fr.derive`, the facade's read-only layer. It holds the column accessors of the list outputs and the row types they are built from. It also holds the row functions, and the texts and order keys every list shares. Use these to read a model yourself and get the same numbers, text and order the outputs print.

## Column accessors

The columns of each list are the `[[lists.<name>.columns]]` tables of the settings, so a settings file can reorder or drop them. Each column has a row `field` and two `[words]` keys: `pdf`, the key of its PDF heading, and `csv`, the key of its CSV header. The lists are `terminal`, `plc`, `bom`, `wires`, `designations`, `connectors`, `cables`, `contents` and `cores`. Each function takes the model first.

- `export_form_of(model)` gives the `[export]` record of a build: the report kinds, the name signs, `data_dir` and the CSV delimiter, encoding, quoting and newline. `export_path(form, name)` is a file's path from `out_dir`, `export_bytes(form, name, text)` its bytes, and `csv_dialect(form)` the `csv` dialect of the CSV form.
- `list_columns(model, name)` gives the row field names the list prints, in order. By default `bom` is `('mpn', 'revision', 'manufacturer', 'description', 'count', 'designations')`, `plc` is `('pin', 'channel_name', 'signal', 'signal_name', 'description', 'wired_to')` and `wires` is `('from_', 'to', 'colour', 'cross_section_mm2', 'label')`. `connectors` holds the connector fields, then the pin fields (`marking`, `net`, `mate_port_designation`, `ends`); a line repeats the connector fields on each pin.
- `list_pdf_columns(model, name)` gives the columns the PDF prints, where they differ from the CSV: `terminal` leaves out `jumper_group`, `cables` leaves out `pairs`, and `connectors` prints the pin fields only. It raises for a list with no `pdf_columns`.
- `list_pdf_heading(model, name, field)` gives the heading a PDF table prints for a column: the `[words]` text of its `pdf` key. It raises when the list has no such column.
- `list_csv_header(model, name, field)` gives the header cell the CSV writes for a column: the `[words]` text of its `csv` key.
- `CELL_SEPARATOR` is `'; '`. It joins the parts of one list cell that holds more than one value, such as several far ends of a terminal. Empty parts are left out.

## Row types

Every row is a frozen record. A row is the one shape an output reads, so the layout and the renderers never look up the model for these facts.

- `CableRow` is one core of one cable, both ends. Fields: `cable`, `cable_designation`, `index`, `colour`, `conductor`, `end_a`, `end_a_designation`, `end_b`, `end_b_designation`. The ends are ports; the designations are their printed text.
- `ConnectorPin` is one pin of a board connector. Fields: `port`, `marking`, `net`, `mate_port`, `mate_port_designation`, `ends`. The `marking` is the port's name. The `net` is the declared net that lists the port, or `None` when none does. The mate's pin is the port of the same name on the mated function. The `ends` are the far ends of every conductor on the pin or on its mate, as a terminal row prints them; empty when there is none.
- `ChannelScaling` is the scaling of a field device, projected so a formatter never looks it up. Fields: `unit`, `raw_min`, `raw_max` (integers), and `eng_min`, `eng_max` (decimals).
- `ConnectorRow` is one connector of a board, as `connector_rows` lists it. Fields: `connector`, `designation`, `style`, `pincount`, `gender`, `mate`, `mate_designation`, `pins`. The `gender` is `None` when the part file states none. The `mate` is `None` when the connector is unmated. The `pins` is a tuple of `ConnectorPin`.
- `DesignationRow` is one line of the designation list. Fields: `item`, `designation`, `reference`, `description`. The `designation` is the printed designation, and `reference` is the reference designation.
- `HarnessCore` is one core of a harness cable, with the label its wire carries. Fields: `conductor`, `index`, `colour`, `label`, `end_a`, `end_a_designation`, `end_b`, `end_b_designation`. The `label` is `None` when the wire has none. Every core of one cable runs from the same physical end to the same other end.
- `HarnessEnd` is one item that a core lands on: a connector housing, a plain device, or a strip of terminals. Fields: `item`, `designation`, `connector`, `style`, `pincount`, `gender`, `mpn`, `pins`. The `designation` is the item's product designation for every end. The connector fields are `None` for a plain device or a strip. When a core lands on a terminal with a parent, `item` is the strip, and `pins` holds one `HarnessPin` per landed terminal.
- `HarnessPin` is one port of a harness end that a core lands on. Fields: `port`, `marking`. The `marking` is the port's own name. For a terminal in a strip it is the bare `group:index` text, such as `L1:1`, without the strip's designation, because the end already prints the strip.
- `PlcChannelRow` is one pin of a PLC channel. Fields: `channel`, `port`, `pin`, `channel_name`, `signal`, `wired_to`, `field_device`, `field_device_designation`, `signal_name`, `description`. The `pin` is the pin's printed designation (`-A2:5`) and `channel_name` the channel's own number. The `wired_to` joins the far ends of that pin's conductors with `CELL_SEPARATOR`, or is `None` when nothing is printed. The `description` is the bound device's `.plc(..., description=)` text, `None` when none was given. The three field fields and `description` are `None` for a channel with no bound device.
- `PlcRackChannel` is one channel of a rack module, bound or spare. Fields: `channel`, `number`, `signal`, `field_device`, `field_device_designation`, `signal_name`, `routing`, `configured`, `scaling`. The field fields are `None` for a spare channel. The `scaling` is `None` when the function that requests the channel (the bound device, else the channel's own function) has no scaling facet. The `signal_name` is the device's request name, else a spare's own name.
- `PlcRackModule` is one PLC module of a rack, with its channels in order. Modules go by `position`, else by their own tag. Channels with one number go by the function names in the part file, in natural order. A block tag never changes the order of racks, modules or channels (model-0259). Fields: `module`, `designation`, `mpn`, `description`, `position`, `channels`. The `mpn` and `description` come from the part. The `position` is `None` when the author never gave one.
- `PlcTable` is one table of the PLC list: the channels of one controller or module. Fields: `item`, `designation` and `rows`. `item` carries the channels, `designation` is its printed designation and the table's heading, and `rows` are its `PlcChannelRow`s in list order, never empty.
- `BoardNetlist` is a board's parts, footprints and nets. Fields: `board`, `board_designation`, `parts`, `nets` and `without_footprint`. `without_footprint` lists the board's parts whose part carries no footprint; a netlist cannot place them, so `parts` omits them. An accessory prints its holder's designation, so it is never listed.
- `NetlistPart` is one placed part of a `BoardNetlist`. Fields: `item`, `designation` (relative to the board), `mpn`, `footprint_library`, `footprint_name` and `installed`. `installed` is the item's own flag: a part not installed stays listed, and the output decides what to do with it.
- `NetlistNet` is one net of a `BoardNetlist`. Fields: `name` and `pins`, the ports it joins.
- `TerminalRow` is one terminal of a strip's connection list. Fields: `terminal`, `designation`, `group`, `index`, `internal`, `external`, `internal_ends`, `external_ends`, `jumper_group`. An unused terminal has empty `internal` and `external` tuples. Bridged terminals share one `jumper_group` number. The `internal_ends[i]` is the far end of `internal[i]`, and the same for `external`.

## Row functions

Each function takes a frozen model and returns rows. None of them writes a file or reads a clock. Most raise a schema error when a named item, function or unit is not in the model, or when an item has no designation. `boards` takes no such check.

- `boards` returns the ids of every item whose part carries a board facet. It sorts them by natural designation, then by id. The export enumeration and the PDF document contents use this same function, so they agree on what a board is.
- `cable_rows` returns one `CableRow` per core of a cable. Cores sort by their index, then by conductor id. Its `unit` keyword keeps the cores drawn by one unit's document.
- `designation_list` returns one `DesignationRow` per item, terminals included, sorted by designation, then id. An accessory that takes its parent's designation has no row. Its `unit` keyword keeps the rows of one unit only; the unit's sole root has no row.
- `board_netlist` takes a model and a board item. It returns the `BoardNetlist` of that board. Its parts are the footprinted descendants of the board. Its nets join the board's internal conductors and its declared nets, never `Mate`s. It raises a schema error when the board is not an item of the model, or when it or a listed item has no designation. Use it to check a board's connectivity yourself; the KiCad export builds the same netlist.
- `plc_channel_rows` returns one `PlcChannelRow` per pin of each PLC channel function, in list order: channels as the PLC list orders them, the pins of a channel by name. Its `unit` keyword keeps one unit's channels. Its `context` keyword sets the location the list prints for, and it has no effect once `unit` is given.
- `plc_tables` returns the rows of `plc_channel_rows`, grouped into one `PlcTable` per carrying item, in the same order. A controller's own channels form its table, the modules' tables follow in rack order, and items in no rack come last, one table each. An item with no channel has no table. Its `unit` and `context` keywords are those of `plc_channel_rows`. Use it when you print one table per controller or module, as the PLC list does.
- `signal_word(model, signal)` returns the word the model's `[words]` gives a `SignalType`; ours are `DI`, `DO`, `AI (V)`, `AI (mA)`, `AO (V)`, `AO (mA)`, `RTD` or `DO (relay)`, and `signal_*` keys of `[words]` change them. The CSV keeps the enum value.
- `plc_list_rows(model, rows)` takes `PlcChannelRow`s and returns one tuple per row, in the `plc` columns' order, for a printed list. The signal is its `signal_word`. A channel with no device and no wire prints the `spare` word of `[words]` as its signal name.
- `terminal_rows` returns one `TerminalRow` per terminal of a strip. Terminals sort by the natural key of their group, then by index, then by id. A far end outside the given `context` prints with its location path in front, such as `+EXT-M1:U1`. A far end inside it prints short, such as `-B12:2/T1`.

- `open_core_rows(model, cable, *, unit=None)` returns one `OpenCoreRow` per open core of `cable`, by core number. An open core is a spare or a screen earthed at one end. A row holds the core's `index`, `colour`, the port it lands on (`at`, `at_designation`; `None` and `""` for none) and `spare`, false for an `SH` screen. `HarnessCable.open_cores` holds the same rows.
- `core_list_rows(model, *, unit=None)` returns one `CoreListRow` per core of every cable `cable_list_rows` lists. The order is the cable list's, then core number. The wired cores and the open ones are in it, and the ends print as the cable drawing prints them. A spare parked on a pin has it as `end_a`. `pair` is `P1` or `screen P1`, `""` outside a pair, and `note` is `spare` for a spare core. `list_columns(model, "cores")` names the fields, in print order. `cores.csv` is this list.
- `contents_rows(cables)` reshapes a tuple of `HarnessCable`s into one `ContentsRow` per cable. The tuple comes from `harness_cables`, `top_level_cables` or `unit_cables`. The row keeps the cable's product facts and adds `ends`. That is every end's designation, in the cable's own order, joined by an en dash, and a blank end drops its dash. `list_columns(model, "contents")` names its columns, in print order.

## Printed texts and order keys

These functions give the one text and the one order that each list uses. A list that prints a label or sorts a column calls them rather than building its own.

- `cable_title` returns the cable's printed title. It is its designation, then a space and its MPN when the cable has one. Without an MPN it is the designation alone.
- `function_designation` renders a function as its item's designation, a colon and the function's name, such as `JB1:J1`. Its `unit` keyword sets whether the text is written for one unit's document or for the whole model.
- `item_description` returns the text a list shows for an item. It is the item's own description, else its part's description, else an empty string. The part's text is never copied onto the item.
- `release_order` returns the order key of a unit release or a history entry, from a version and a revision as two integers. The key is a pair of integers, so revision 10 sorts after revision 9. Compare releases with this key, never with printed text, because the text `"1.10"` sorts before `"1.9"`.
- `sideless_pins` gives the pins of two series ends that have no line side, each in pin order, as `SidelessPins(first, second, problem)`. It takes a label and a tuple of port templates for each end. The order is the marking by value, and the pin's name when it prints none. `problem` is the message that says why the ends cannot pair, or `None`. They cannot pair with a different number of pins, or the same names in another order. A series between two connectors pairs their pins with it.

---

<!-- source: https://olejbondahl.github.io/fransys/0.23.5/guide/reading-records/index.md -->

# Reading: records, lookups and ratings

This page covers the records that describe a model's structure, the lookups that find them,
and the ratings and currents that say what a circuit may carry. Each record type has a
table function that returns every record of that type, keyed by id. Every name here is
reached as `fr.derive.NAME`.

## Records

- `Aspect` is one of the three IEC 81346 views of the same objects: `FUNCTION`, `PRODUCT` and `LOCATION`.
- `AspectNode` is a node in one aspect tree. Its fields are `id`, `key`, `aspect`, `parent` (an `AspectNode` id, or `None` at the root), `label`, `description` and `ext`. A `LOCATION` node with label `C1` is the place `+C1`. The table is `aspect_nodes`.
- `Placement` puts one item at one aspect node. Its fields are `id`, `key`, `item`, `node` and `ext`. An item has at most one placement per aspect, so one item can have a product placement and a location placement. The table is `placements`.
- `Boundary` marks a function as part of a unit's interface. Its fields are `id`, `key`, `unit`, `function`, `name` and `ext`. `name` is the field name the unit gave the function, or `None`. One function can be the boundary of several units. The table is `boundaries`.
- `Port` is a connection point on a function. Its fields are `id`, `key`, `function`, `template`, `name`, `role`, `marking` and `ext`. `template` is `None` for a port without a part template. The `marking` field is the pin text printed on the drawing: `None` prints the port's name, an empty string prints nothing, and any other string prints as given.
